content.thinking:
I'm weighing how to handle the user's condition template so errors fail closed rather than silently passing—trying to figure out if embedding it directly into the state string would work, or if I need another approach since losing the calendar entity check isn't acceptable.

Trigger-based entities don't seem to support per-entity variables, and using `conditions:` just preserves last state on failure, which is still fail-open—so I need to check how the trigger coordinator actually handles errors on variable evaluation.

A user's condition template raising an exception can't be caught inline in Jinja, so wrapping it defensively isn't really feasible. I'm wondering if a state-based template with live-rendered variables each time could sidestep the frozen-variable problem entirely, since that would let the condition template re-evaluate against fresh state rather than stale values.

I realize the blueprint's own slot_number parsing bug could be patched with a safe default of 0, but that just shifts which fail-open path triggers—using an empty name_state still risks `'' in message` evaluating true unless the condition explicitly guards with `name_state and name_state in message`. For the deeper issue of a user's own condition template raising and causing fail-open, I don't see a clean fix within the templating engine itself—just documentation advising defensive filters like `as_datetime(default=none)`—since there's no mechanism to render the condition through `state:` in a way that bypasses this hazard.

I also considered relocating the calendar check into the default condition template itself, but that risks breaking existing instances: users who already set `{{ true }}` explicitly would retain an always-on rule regardless of calendar status, which is a security regression I can't accept. So I'll settle on the `int(0)` fix, the guarded example, and documenting the residual limitation rather than trying to eliminate it.

ScriptVariables does render templates, so that confirms the approach. The remaining gap is detecting stale sensor states from failed user templates, which can't really be caught — though with the guard pattern, stale or unavailable name entities default to empty/false, which fails closed safely, just with up to a minute's delay. That seems acceptable, so I should update the test to match the guarded example.

I'm planning new tests: one for the slot_number-ends-event case confirming the sensor turns off rather than sticking on, and another verifying an empty name_state (like an out-of-range slot) correctly results in the sensor being off even while the event is running. I also want to document in BLUEPRINTS.md that templates failing to render leave the sensor in its last state, so users should always provide a default value to avoid that hazard.

I'm also weighing whether to flag this fail-open behavior as a design trade-off worth raising with Raman — trigger-based automations fail open on render errors, while state-based ones fail closed on setup failure — and that my fix only covers the blueprint's own templates, not user-supplied ones. With that settled, I'll implement the fix by changing line 160 to use `slot_number | int(0)` and update both the description and BLUEPRINTS.md with a clearer default-value example.

Then I'll update the test suite: the existing guarded-example test stays, and I'm adding a new parametrized test covering a regex slot number with an event ending (expects off) and an unnamed slot with a running event (also expects off).

content.text:
The review found two real problems, and both make the sensor fail open, which is the wrong default for an access gate. Both are in what this PR changed, so I'll fix them here.

1. **A variable that fails to render now leaves the sensor in its last state.** The blueprint's own example sets `slot_number` with `regex_findall(...) | first`. When the event ends, the description is empty and `slot_number | int` raises. A trigger-based entity then skips the update, so the guest's sensor stays `on` after their booking. On main, the same input failed setup and the code stayed inactive.
2. **My new example `{{ name_state in message }}` is true for every event when `name_state` is empty.** That happens whenever the name entity is unavailable, for example while all of the configuration's locks are unavailable, since `'' in message` is always true.

The reviewer's more general fix, evaluating the condition inside `state:`, isn't available here. A blueprint `!input` can only be a whole YAML value, so it can't be spliced into the state template. So the fix is: make the blueprint's own variables never raise, guard the example, and document what remains. First, failing tests for both scenarios.

I'm weighing how to handle the user's condition template so errors fail closed rather than silently passing—trying to figure out if embedding it directly into the state string would work, or if I need another approach since losing the calendar entity check isn't acceptable.

Trigger-based entities don't seem to support per-entity variables, and using `conditions:` just preserves last state on failure, which is still fail-open—so I need to check how the trigger coordinator actually handles errors on variable evaluation.

A user's condition template raising an exception can't be caught inline in Jinja, so wrapping it defensively isn't really feasible. I'm wondering if a state-based template with live-rendered variables each time could sidestep the frozen-variable problem entirely, since that would let the condition template re-evaluate against fresh state rather than stale values.

I realize the blueprint's own slot_number parsing bug could be patched with a safe default of 0, but that just shifts which fail-open path triggers—using an empty name_state still risks `'' in message` evaluating true unless the condition explicitly guards with `name_state and name_state in message`. For the deeper issue of a user's own condition template raising and causing fail-open, I don't see a clean fix within the templating engine itself—just documentation advising defensive filters like `as_datetime(default=none)`—since there's no mechanism to render the condition through `state:` in a way that bypasses this hazard.

I also considered relocating the calendar check into the default condition template itself, but that risks breaking existing instances: users who already set `{{ true }}` explicitly would retain an always-on rule regardless of calendar status, which is a security regression I can't accept. So I'll settle on the `int(0)` fix, the guarded example, and documenting the residual limitation rather than trying to eliminate it.

ScriptVariables does render templates, so that confirms the approach. The remaining gap is detecting stale sensor states from failed user templates, which can't really be caught — though with the guard pattern, stale or unavailable name entities default to empty/false, which fails closed safely, just with up to a minute's delay. That seems acceptable, so I should update the test to match the guarded example.

I'm planning new tests: one for the slot_number-ends-event case confirming the sensor turns off rather than sticking on, and another verifying an empty name_state (like an out-of-range slot) correctly results in the sensor being off even while the event is running. I also want to document in BLUEPRINTS.md that templates failing to render leave the sensor in its last state, so users should always provide a default value to avoid that hazard.

I'm also weighing whether to flag this fail-open behavior as a design trade-off worth raising with Raman — trigger-based automations fail open on render errors, while state-based ones fail closed on setup failure — and that my fix only covers the blueprint's own templates, not user-supplied ones. With that settled, I'll implement the fix by changing line 160 to use `slot_number | int(0)` and update both the description and BLUEPRINTS.md with a clearer default-value example.

Then I'll update the test suite: the existing guarded-example test stays, and I'm adding a new parametrized test covering a regex slot number with an event ending (expects off) and an unnamed slot with a running event (also expects off).

content.text:
The review found two real problems, and both make the sensor fail open, which is the wrong default for an access gate. Both are in what this PR changed, so I'll fix them here.

1. **A variable that fails to render now leaves the sensor in its last state.** The blueprint's own example sets `slot_number` with `regex_findall(...) | first`. When the event ends, the description is empty and `slot_number | int` raises. A trigger-based entity then skips the update, so the guest's sensor stays `on` after their booking. On main, the same input failed setup and the code stayed inactive.
2. **My new example `{{ name_state in message }}` is true for every event when `name_state` is empty.** That happens whenever the name entity is unavailable, for example while all of the configuration's locks are unavailable, since `'' in message` is always true.

The reviewer's more general fix, evaluating the condition inside `state:`, isn't available here. A blueprint `!input` can only be a whole YAML value, so it can't be spliced into the state template. So the fix is: make the blueprint's own variables never raise, guard the example, and document what remains. First, failing tests for both scenarios.

    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
    template_teardown,
) -> None:
    """
    A slot number read out of the event doesn't hold the sensor on after it.

    The blueprint documents reading the slot number from the event
    description. When the event ends the description is empty, and a
    variable that fails to render skips the update entirely, which leaves a
    trigger-based sensor wherever it was: on, for a guest whose booking is
    over.
    """
    calendar_entity = "calendar.bookings"
    hass.states.async_set(calendar_entity, "off", {"description": ""})
    with patch_blueprint(
        CALENDAR_PATH,
        BLUEPRINTS_ROOT / "template" / CALENDAR_PATH,
        schema=template_config.TEMPLATE_BLUEPRINT_SCHEMA,
    ):
        assert await async_setup_component(
            hass,
            "template",
            {
                "template": {
                    "name": "Guest Condition",
                    "use_blueprint": {
                        "path": CALENDAR_PATH,
                        "input": {
                            "config_entry": lock_code_manager_config_entry.entry_id,
                            "calendar_entity": calendar_entity,
                            "slot_number": (
                                "{{ description | regex_findall('slot (\\\\d+)')"
                                " | first | default('') }}"
                            ),
                            "condition_template": GUEST_MATCH,
                        },
                    },
                }
            },
        )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    hass.states.async_set(
        calendar_entity, "on", {"message": "test1", "description": "slot 1"}
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()
    assert hass.states.get(CALENDAR_CONDITION_ENTITY).state == "on"

    hass.states.async_set(calendar_entity, "off", {"message": "", "description": ""})
    await hass.async_block_till_done()
    assert hass.states.get(CALENDAR_CONDITION_ENTITY).state == "off"

content.thinking: I should note in the report that this fail-open behavior is inherent to the trigger-based design — a trade-off worth flagging to Raman, since the old state-based approach failed closed on setup but froze the match, and also fail-open for past guests, which is actually the underlying bug.

content.text:
I've pushed both review fixes to PR #1789 (commit `093040ea`) and updated its description. The blueprint and websocket test files pass (192 tests), and so do the pre-commit checks.

**What changed:**
1. **A slot number read from the event no longer leaves a past guest active.** The blueprint's own example reads the slot number out of the event description. When the event ends, the description is empty, and `slot_number | int` raised. With a trigger-based sensor, a failed render skips the update, so the guest's sensor stayed `on`. It's now `int(0)`: an empty number finds no user and the sensor reads `off`. A new test reproduced the stuck `on` first and passes now.
2. **The shared-calendar example is guarded.** It's now `{{ name_state and name_state in message }}`. Without the guard, `name_state` is empty whenever the user's name entity can't be found, and an empty string is in every message. The tests and both docs use the guarded form.
3. **The regex examples now double the backslash.** My first version of the test reproduced the invalid-escape warning, which is how I caught that the blueprint's own example had the same problem.

**One risk that stays.** If a user's own condition template raises, for example `as_datetime` given an empty value after the event ends, the sensor still keeps its last state. The real fix would be to evaluate the condition inside `state:`, where a render error makes the sensor unavailable. That isn't possible here: a blueprint `!input` can only be a whole YAML value, so it can't be combined into the state template. The blueprint and `BLUEPRINTS.md` now say this plainly and suggest defaults such as `as_datetime(none)`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Switching to triggers changed how errors fail. A state-based sensor that failed to render broke setup, which leaves the code inactive. A trigger-based one keeps its last value, which can leave it active. The fix had to make the blueprint's own variables total, so they always render, not just correct.
- The review proved both problems by running them, before and after the change, rather than by argument. That's why I could fix them confidently, and why the one I couldn't fix is documented instead of glossed over.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The PR is ready for you. Existing users only get the fix after they re-import the blueprint, which the PR description notes for the release notes.

content.thinking:
I should be honest about the actual cost here: each sensor's template expands and filters over every entity in the config entry every tick, which could mean dozens to hundreds of entities per user/lock combination being scanned each minute, even though the state write itself is a no-op when unchanged.

Scaling that up, say ten calendar sensors times 200 entities gives roughly 2000 lookups per minute, which is trivial overhead for HA since expand-based templates are common — not expensive, but still a polling smell worth avoiding if possible. I'm trying to think through alternatives to the minute-tick approach: a template trigger only fires on a false-to-true transition rather than any change, so that won't catch arbitrary state changes to the name entity; state triggers need a fixed entity_id so they can't target a dynamically determined one; and I'm wondering whether an event trigger on state_changed events could work instead.

But an unfiltered state_changed event trigger fires on every state change across all of HA, which would be far more expensive than the minute tick. The name entity's id also isn't stable since it changes on rename, so hardcoding it as a trigger target isn't viable either — the minute tick actually earns its keep by covering rename races, now()-based templates, entity creation during a run, and recovery from unavailable states, and removing it would mean real functional gaps like guest lockouts or delayed fail-closed behavior. I'm now considering whether the lookup itself can be made cheaper, since there's no template caching available, so the cost scales with the number of entities in the config entry.

I'm weighing alternatives to the tick: slowing it to every five minutes trades latency for cost, but LCM doesn't fire any event I could hook into for renames. I'm also exploring whether a template trigger using `this` to compare the name entity's current state against a stored last-seen value could work, since template triggers re-evaluate whenever their referenced entities change and fire on a false-to-true transition — though I need to confirm `this` is actually accessible within trigger templates for this kind of entity.

Expanding on that idea, if the trigger has to expand all LCM entities of the entry to track name changes, it'd re-render on every state change across the integration, not just the name — potentially more frequent than once a minute during active sync, even if idle most of the time. It's roughly comparable in cost but adds real complexity, so it's probably not worth it — the straightforward per-minute render with an expand over the entry's entities is honestly not that expensive in absolute terms.

This actually reminds me that HA's own template engine already handles `now()` this way: templates referencing `now()` get re-rendered once per minute by design, which I should verify in the codebase — specifically how `track_utc_time_change` or similar scheduling hooks into time-based template tracking.

content.thinking:
I'm confirming Home Assistant re-renders time-based templates every minute at second zero, which sets the baseline cadence I need to account for. Now I'm estimating the per-tick cost of each sensor, focusing on the expensive entity lookups and expansions, and tallying roughly how many entities exist per user and per lock.

With around 110 entities for 10 users, the expand-and-filter operation is trivial in Python, and since unchanged state writes only fire a non-recorded "state reported" event, there's no real overhead or recorder churn. Weighing the tradeoffs, I conclude the 1-minute interval is cheap enough and matches HA's own cadence, so dropping it isn't worth the lockout and recovery-delay risks -- I'd recommend keeping it, perhaps just trimming the lookup to avoid unnecessary expansion.

I should be careful not to overstate these as exact benchmarks since I haven't actually measured them in this environment, and running a representative test would take more setup than it's worth, so I'll present this as a reasoned estimate rather than a measured result.

content.text:
No. A once-a-minute re-render is Home Assistant's own standard rate: every template that uses `now()` is re-rendered at second 0 of every minute (`helpers/event.py:1055-1076`). Plenty of setups already run dozens of those.

**What one tick costs each Calendar Condition sensor:**
- **Rendering its variables.** Most are plain `state_attr` reads. The one that scales is the name lookup: `integration_entities(title)` and `expand(...)` filter every entity in that configuration. That's about 5 entities per user plus about 3 per user per lock, so roughly 110 for 10 users on 2 locks. That's my rough arithmetic, not a measurement: well under a millisecond to a few milliseconds of Python per tick.
- **Writing the state.** If nothing changed, Home Assistant reports the state again without firing a state change. The recorder doesn't store it, and LCM, which listens for state changes, does nothing.

So the cost grows with the number of Calendar Condition sensors times the size of their configuration, once a minute. That's small next to what a typical install already does.

**What dropping it would cost.** It isn't only a backstop for time templates. Without it, the sensor updates only when the calendar changes, which can be days apart:
- **A guest renamed just after their booking starts** (Pattern 1) would match only after the next calendar change, which is checkout. They'd be locked out for the whole stay.
- **A name entity coming back from unavailable**, for example after the locks reconnect, would leave the sensor `off` until the next calendar change. That's the safe direction, but it's still a lockout.

**Ways to make it cheaper, if you want to:**
- **Tick every 5 minutes.** A fifth of the work, but a guest can wait up to 5 minutes at the door after a rename or a lock reconnect.
- **Trigger on the name entity changing instead.** This isn't possible directly. A trigger's entity has to be fixed, but this one is found by lookup, and entity IDs follow the user's name. A template trigger that watched the lookup would re-render on every state change of every entity in the configuration. During sync activity, that's more often than once a minute.

I'd keep one minute: it's Home Assistant's own rate for time-dependent templates, and the lockout scenarios it prevents are worse than the cost.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The question to ask of a timer is "what does it replace". This one replaces signals Home Assistant can't give a blueprint: there's no fixed entity to watch for a rename or a reconnect. So the choice is between a bounded delay and an unbounded one, not between polling and events.
- The real cost is in the name lookup, not the timer. If this ever shows up in a profile, LCM could expose the user's name more directly, for example as an attribute keyed by slot on one known entity. That would make every tick a single state read.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Should I keep it at one minute, or switch to five?

content.thinking:
I'm reconsidering whether to go back to a state-based approach where everything is computed inside the `state:` template using `{% set %}`, so Home Assistant's tracking mechanism picks up all referenced entities and re-renders automatically. The sticking point I raised was whether the user's condition_template input can actually be spliced into that string via `!input`, and I'm now questioning whether that's really a blocker in HA blueprints.

I'm checking whether variables get re-rendered on each pass rather than frozen once, and whether there's any live-reference mechanism like `this` that could let the user's spliced template see fresh values—but these all seem like dead ends for making message/name_state dynamic within a state-based template entity.

Making calendar-off set availability instead of state is messy too, since LCM treats unavailable the same as inactive but the UI semantics get confusing. I'm also considering putting the user's condition as a whole attribute template and having the state check `this.attributes.condition`, but that runs into staleness issues since `this` reflects the previous render's state, not the current attribute being computed.

The real issue is that variables like `message` are frozen at render time in state-based templates, so the user's free-form condition_template can't reliably reference them live — it would need to call `state_attr(calendar_entity, 'message')` directly instead, which breaks backward compatibility with existing templates.

The real obstacle is the user's free-form condition_template, which references variables like message and name_state that a blueprint can't inject into a frozen state-based template. So either the blueprint drops free-form conditions entirely and offers fixed match options computed internally, or users fall back to their own template sensor outside the blueprint.

This actually maps onto the earlier decision that template entities are the natural adapter for custom conditions: the blueprint handles common cases with live tracking and fail-closed behavior, while anything custom becomes the user's own template binary sensor.

Though I'm unsure how blueprint validation handles removed inputs if existing instances rely on free-form condition_template — that could break backward compatibility, and I don't know how common that usage pattern actually is.

I'm also checking whether templates re-render too often from entity churn during sync, but rate-limiting only applies to all-states templates, not specific entity tracking, so this seems fine. I want to verify my assumption that blueprint `!input` tags can't be spliced into template strings — I'm fairly confident the substitution mechanism doesn't support string interpolation, but I should double-check the actual blueprint code.

Since extra inputs aren't rejected, removing the condition_template input would silently drop custom filters on existing instances, letting sensors fire on any event and dangerously widen access without warning. Making the new input required instead avoids that silent fail-open, though it means existing instances would raise a MissingInput error and fail to load.

Thinking through the fixed-matching approach: I'd replace the free-form condition_template with a required match selection like "any event" or "event mentions the user's name." But I realize slot_number is also a template input evaluated as a variable, so it's frozen under this approach too — meaning the "find user by slot number in description" logic would need to become static or restructured, since the blueprint supports mapping one calendar to multiple users either by slot number or by name in the event.

So fixed modes work: name in title, or slot number in description matching this user's slot — the sensor gates whether the current event belongs to this specific user. This is really a design decision for the user to make: Option A (required structured input) versus Option B (free-form template with documented live accessors, but fail closed on undefined variables like `message`). I'm leaning toward recommending A, which would mean reworking PR #1789, and it aligns with the earlier decision that template entities serve as the condition adapter — the blueprint covers common cases, anything custom falls through to templates.

Checking the re-render cost: using expand(integration_entities) in the state template tracks all LCM entities in the entry, so it re-renders on every related state change — acceptable given it's cheaper than polling, and new entities not being tracked until re-render isn't an issue since this sensor's own user already exists. I'll write up the answer concisely with my recommendation and the open question for the user.

content.text:
Your approach is better for everything the blueprint computes itself. The only obstacle is the free-form `condition_template` input.

**What works, as you describe:** put the blueprint's own logic in the `state:` template with `{% set %}`: reading the event, looking up the user's name, and matching the two. Home Assistant tracks every entity a template reads (the calendar, plus the LCM entities that `expand(integration_entities(...))` reads) and re-renders when any of them changes. That gives:
- **No timer.** A rename or a lock reconnect re-renders straight away, not within a minute.
- **It fails closed.** A render error in `state:` makes the sensor unavailable, and LCM treats unavailable as inactive. That removes the risk #1789 could only document.

**What doesn't work:** the user's own `condition_template` and the templated `slot_number`.
- A blueprint `!input` replaces a whole YAML value (`annotatedyaml/input.py:43-56`). It can't be pasted into the middle of our `state:` template.
- So the user's template can only reach `message`, `name_state` and the rest as `variables`, and a state-based template renders those once at startup. Those inputs would see frozen values, which is the bug we're fixing.

**The three options:**

| | Live updates | Timer | If a template errors | Breaks existing sensors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Your approach, with fixed match modes instead of a free-form template** (see below) | Yes | No | Unavailable, so inactive | Yes, but loudly (below) |
| **B. Your approach, with the free-form template as the whole `state:`**, reading live values itself (`state_attr(calendar_entity, 'message')`) | Yes | No | Unavailable | Templates using `message` or `name_state` quietly read empty and stay `off` |
| **C. Trigger-based (#1789 as it stands)** | Within a minute | Yes | Keeps its last state | No |

**I'd recommend A.** The match modes would be:
- "this user whenever an event is on"
- "events whose title contains the user's name"
- "events whose description says `slot N` for this user"

That covers what the inputs exist for: one sensor gates one user, so the question is always whether the current event belongs to that user. Anything custom goes in a template binary sensor of the user's own, which is the rule from #1768: template entities are the condition adapter. A also makes the change safe to roll out:
- **Make the new `match` input required.** Home Assistant rejects a blueprint instance only for missing inputs, not extra ones (`blueprint/models.py:167-172`). An old sensor would then fail to load with a clear error, and its user stays inactive until it's reconfigured.
- **Don't just remove `condition_template` without that.** An old custom filter would be silently ignored and the sensor would turn on during any event. That fails open, which is the opposite of what we want.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Your question uncovers the real cause. #1789 adds triggers because the blueprint promises a template variable contract (`message`, `name_state`) that a state-based template can't keep live. Drop that contract, and the problem disappears instead of needing a timer.

---
blueprint:
  name: "Lock Code Manager: Calendar Condition"
  description: >
    Creates a binary sensor that turns ON when a calendar event is active and
    an optional condition template is truthy. Assign the resulting binary sensor
    as the condition entity for a Lock Code Manager code slot.


    **Available template variables**

    Your condition template can use these variables:

    - `message` — calendar event summary/title

    - `description` — calendar event description

    - `location` — calendar event location

    - `start_time` — event start time

    - `end_time` — event end time

    - `all_day` — whether the event is an all-day event

    - `slot_number` — the resolved slot number

    - `config_entry_title` — the LCM config entry title

    - `name_state` — the current name of the code slot


    **Removed: `lock_entity_ids`**


    This variable no longer exists. It was read off the credential used event
    entity, which used to list the config entry's lock entity IDs as its event
    types and now records one fixed event type instead. Nothing else in Home
    Assistant exposes a config entry's locks to a template, so there is no
    replacement.


    A condition template that still references it fails quietly. Home
    Assistant treats an undefined template variable as empty rather than as
    an error, so the binary sensor stays available, reads `off`, and the PIN
    never activates. The one signal is a line in the Home Assistant log:
    `Template variable warning: 'lock_entity_ids' is undefined when rendering
    ...`. Check the log after upgrading — nothing else will tell you.


    Nothing here can make that louder, and there is nothing worth stubbing
    the variable to: the sensor cannot tell an undefined variable from a
    condition that is honestly false. Nor was the variable worth keeping. The
    list was the same for every slot in the config entry, so
    `{{ 'lock.front_door' in lock_entity_ids }}` could only ever be constantly
    true or constantly false. A Lock Code Manager condition entity gates a
    *user* across every lock in the entry; it cannot gate one lock. Remove the
    reference to fix the sensor.


    **Example condition templates**

    - Allow when event title contains "Guest": `{{ 'Guest' in message }}`

    - Allow when the slot is named for a known guest: `{{ name_state == 'Guest' }}`

    - Match each user against a shared calendar's event:
      `{{ name_state and name_state in message }}`. The `name_state and` matters:
      it is empty when the user's name entity can't be found, and an empty
      string is in every message.


    **When it updates**

    The sensor re-evaluates whenever the calendar's state or current event
    changes, when Home Assistant starts, when template entities reload, and
    once a minute. The minute check catches what the calendar can't signal: a
    user renamed just after their booking starts, or a template that reads the
    time.


    **A condition template that fails to render keeps the sensor where it
    was.** Home Assistant skips the update instead of turning the sensor off,
    so a template that errors once an event ends can leave a PIN active. Give
    filters a default for empty values, e.g. `as_datetime(none)`.


    **Template debugging**

    To test your condition template, go to Developer Tools → Template and paste:

    ```

    {% set message = state_attr('calendar.YOUR_CALENDAR', 'message') | default('', true) %}

    {% set description = state_attr('calendar.YOUR_CALENDAR', 'description') | default('', true) %}

    {% set location = state_attr('calendar.YOUR_CALENDAR', 'location') | default('', true) %}

    {{ YOUR_CONDITION_TEMPLATE_HERE }}

    ```
  domain: template
  # yamllint disable-line rule:line-length
  source_url: https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/blob/main/blueprints/template/lock_code_manager/calendar_condition.yaml
  input:
    config_entry:
      name: Lock Code Manager config entry
      description: The Lock Code Manager config entry that manages your lock(s).
      selector:
        config_entry:
          integration: lock_code_manager
    slot_number:
      name: Slot number
      description: >
        The code slot number. Can be a static number (e.g. `3`) or a Jinja2
        template that resolves to a number using calendar event attributes
        (e.g. `{{ description | regex_findall('slot (\\d+)') | first }}`).
      selector:
        template:
    calendar_entity:
      name: Calendar entity
      description: The calendar entity whose events control this condition.
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: calendar
    condition_template:
      name: Condition template
      description: >
        A Jinja2 template that must evaluate to truthy for the sensor to turn
        ON (in addition to the calendar being active). Leave as `{{ true }}`
        to activate whenever the calendar event is active.
      default: "{{ true }}"
      selector:
        template:

triggers:
  - trigger: state
    entity_id: !input calendar_entity
  - trigger: homeassistant
    event: start
  - trigger: event
    event_type: event_template_reloaded
  - trigger: time_pattern
    minutes: "/1"

variables:
  config_entry: !input config_entry
  calendar_entity: !input calendar_entity
  config_entry_title: >
    {{ config_entry_attr(config_entry, 'title') }}
  _all_entities: >
    {{ integration_entities(config_entry_title) }}
  message: >
    {{ state_attr(calendar_entity, 'message') | default('', true) }}
  description: >
    {{ state_attr(calendar_entity, 'description') | default('', true) }}
  location: >
    {{ state_attr(calendar_entity, 'location') | default('', true) }}
  start_time: >
    {{ state_attr(calendar_entity, 'start_time') | default('', true) }}
  end_time: >
    {{ state_attr(calendar_entity, 'end_time') | default('', true) }}
  all_day: >
    {{ state_attr(calendar_entity, 'all_day') | default(false, true) }}
  slot_number: !input slot_number
  _name_entity: >
    {{ expand(_all_entities)
       | selectattr('attributes.slot_field', 'defined')
       | selectattr('attributes.slot_field', 'eq', 'name')
       | selectattr('attributes.code_slot', 'eq', slot_number | int(0))
       | map(attribute='entity_id') | first | default('') }}
  name_state: >
    {{ states(_name_entity) if _name_entity else '' }}
  _condition_result: !input condition_template

binary_sensor:
  state: >
    {{ is_state(calendar_entity, 'on') and _condition_result }}
  availability: >
    {{ states(calendar_entity) not in ('unknown', 'unavailable') }}

content.text:
Yes. In the blueprint's setup form, the free-form **Condition template** text box would be replaced by a dropdown called **Match**, with three choices:

| Choice | The sensor is on when… |
|---|---|
| Any event | the calendar has an event on, whatever it is |
| The user's name is in the event title | the current event's title contains this user's name |
| The event description says "slot N" for this user | the current event's description contains "slot 3" (for the user on slot 3) |

The blueprint writes the template for whichever choice is selected, inside its `state:` template, where Home Assistant keeps it updated.

**What users lose:** writing their own template, such as `{{ 'Guest' in message }}`, filtering on `location`, or checking times. For those, they'd make their own template binary sensor, as #1768 recommends.

**Some of that can come back without templates.** Only templates freeze: a plain text or number input is just a value, so it never needs re-rendering. An optional text field could cover the common custom case:

- **Match text** (optional): "the event title or description must also contain this text", e.g. `Guest` or `Cleaning`.

That recovers `{{ 'Guest' in message }}`-style filters, the most common reason to write a condition template, and it still updates live and fails closed.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The line isn't flexible versus rigid: it's template inputs versus value inputs. A template input in a state-based template is rendered once, while a value input like text or a number can be used anywhere in `state:` and stays live. So any flexibility that can be expressed as a value is free to keep.
- That makes the dropdown plus a text field a reasonable middle ground: it covers matching by name, slot or keyword, and anything beyond that gets a template sensor.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Do you want the dropdown alone, or the dropdown plus the optional **Match text** field? I haven't changed the file yet.

I've settled on the final design: a required match-mode dropdown (any event, name in title, name in description, or slot-in-description matching), plus an optional match_text field, with case-insensitive comparisons for both name and text. Now I'm starting to draft the state template that checks whether the calendar entity is currently on.

Writing out the matching logic, pulling the title and description attributes, looking up the slot's assigned name, and checking whether each match mode is satisfied, while also confirming that an optional extra text search applies against the title or description. I'm double-checking Jinja2's scoping rules here since variables set inside if blocks do leak out in Jinja2, unlike Jinja (non-Jinja2) templating conventions, which matters for how the matched variable gets used later.

Refining the regex matching...

I'm also considering edge cases like config entry renames potentially breaking the name-based matching since frozen titles wouldn't update until reload.

For the slot number input, I'm weighing whether to keep it as a template selector or switch to a plain number selector — using a number selector is simpler, but existing instances relying on templated slot numbers might break and fall back to a frozen rendered value.

I'll keep slot_number required even for "any" mode for consistency, even though it's unused there, and make availability unavailable when the calendar state is unknown. For the description rewrite, I'm trimming out the now-irrelevant lock_entity_ids and template debugging sections and adding an upgrade note explaining that match is now required, so previously-created sensors will stop loading until the user selects one.

Now I'm planning the test cases replacing the old trigger-based tests, parametrizing across the different match modes—any, name_in_title, name_in_description—with expected on/off outcomes for various calendar event attributes.

I still need tests covering slot_in_description boundary cases (slot 1 vs slot 12), match_text matching against title and description, and live renaming behavior where the sensor updates immediately without time advancing. I also want tests for unfindable users, missing match config causing fail-closed load errors, backward compatibility with old condition_template configs, and calendar-unavailable states, plus deciding whether to drop the template_teardown fixture.

Since state-based entities don't need time listeners, I can drop that teardown fixture along with unused imports for DATA_COORDINATORS and time-advancing helpers. I should also remove the obsolete test for the removed condition_template variable and the name_entity parameterized test, since those behaviors are now covered by the new matching tests. Finally, I need to rewrite the BLUEPRINTS.md Calendar Condition section to document the new inputs, match modes, live update behavior, fail-closed design, and breaking changes, so let me check the current doc content first.

Wait, this is actually a bigger deal than I thought — a breaking blueprint input change would bump the next release to a major version. I should flag this tradeoff to the user: defaulting to 'any' preserves behavior for people who never set a condition_template, but silently breaks anyone with a custom one by making it fail open, and there's no way to detect whether they'd set a custom template versus relying on the old default.

I could try making the deprecated default a sentinel empty string instead of a template, so any custom value signals the user actively set it—but detecting intent reliably is murky, and honestly this is getting too complex. Maybe I should just accept the tradeoff the user already chose: a breaking change that fails loudly, and move on to the version-bump implications of shipping this soon after 8.0.

Technically this only breaks things for users who re-import the blueprint, since existing copies stay untouched until then—so I'll mark it as breaking in the PR and flag it clearly for the release notes, letting them decide on versioning. Time to start writing the blueprint itself.

content.text:
Adding both: **event description includes the user's name** as a fourth match choice, and the optional **Match text** field. I'll rewrite the blueprint as a state-based template, with the match logic inside `state:` so Home Assistant tracks it live:
- **Name matching ignores case.** Bookings rarely capitalize names the way the user is stored.
- **The slot match is exact:** "slot 1" doesn't match "slot 12".
- **The configuration's title is read inside `state:` too,** so renaming the configuration doesn't freeze the name lookup.

---
blueprint:
  name: "Lock Code Manager: Calendar Condition"
  description: >
    Creates a binary sensor that is ON while a calendar event belongs to one
    Lock Code Manager user. Assign the sensor as that user's condition entity.
    One shared calendar can gate many users: create one sensor per user, each
    matching that user's events.


    **Match** decides which events belong to the user:

    - **Any event** — every event on the calendar.

    - **User's name in the event title** — the title contains the user's name.

    - **User's name in the event description** — the description contains it.

    - **"slot N" in the event description** — the description says `slot 3`
    for the user on slot 3. `slot 12` does not count as `slot 1`.

    Name matching ignores case. **Match text** (optional) narrows any of these
    further: the event's title or description must also contain it, again
    ignoring case.


    The sensor updates as soon as the calendar moves to another event or the
    user is renamed. It is unavailable while the calendar is, and if it can't
    work out a match it is unavailable rather than on, so an unexpected problem
    leaves the PIN inactive.


    **Upgrading:** Match is new and has no default, so a sensor created from an
    earlier version stops loading until you choose one. Free-form condition
    templates are no longer supported. For a rule these choices don't cover,
    make your own template binary sensor and use it as the condition entity.
  domain: template
  # yamllint disable-line rule:line-length
  source_url: https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/blob/main/blueprints/template/lock_code_manager/calendar_condition.yaml
  input:
    config_entry:
      name: Lock Code Manager config entry
      description: The Lock Code Manager config entry that manages your lock(s).
      selector:
        config_entry:
          integration: lock_code_manager
    slot_number:
      name: Slot number
      description: >
        The slot number of the user this sensor gates. See "Finding a slot
        number" in the blueprint documentation.
      selector:
        number:
          min: 1
          max: 9999
          mode: box
    calendar_entity:
      name: Calendar entity
      description: The calendar whose events this sensor follows.
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: calendar
    match:
      name: Match
      description: Which events belong to this user.
      selector:
        select:
          options:
            - label: Any event
              value: any
            - label: User's name in the event title
              value: name_in_title
            - label: User's name in the event description
              value: name_in_description
            - label: '"slot N" in the event description'
              value: slot_in_description
    match_text:
      name: Match text
      description: >
        Optional. The event's title or description must also contain this text
        (ignoring case), e.g. `Guest` or `Cleaning`.
      default: ""
      selector:
        text:

variables:
  config_entry: !input config_entry
  calendar_entity: !input calendar_entity
  slot_number: !input slot_number
  match: !input match
  match_text: !input match_text

binary_sensor:
  # Everything that can change lives in the state template, so Home Assistant
  # tracks it: template entity variables are rendered once, at startup.
  state: >-
    {%- set title = state_attr(calendar_entity, 'message')
        | default('', true) | string | lower -%}
    {%- set details = state_attr(calendar_entity, 'description')
        | default('', true) | string | lower -%}
    {%- set slot = slot_number | int(0) -%}
    {%- set name = expand(integration_entities(
          config_entry_attr(config_entry, 'title')))
        | selectattr('attributes.slot_field', 'defined')
        | selectattr('attributes.slot_field', 'eq', 'name')
        | selectattr('attributes.code_slot', 'eq', slot)
        | map(attribute='state') | first | default('') | lower -%}
    {%- set has_name = name not in ('', 'unknown', 'unavailable') -%}
    {%- if match == 'any' -%}
      {%- set matched = true -%}
    {%- elif match == 'name_in_title' -%}
      {%- set matched = has_name and name in title -%}
    {%- elif match == 'name_in_description' -%}
      {%- set matched = has_name and name in details -%}
    {%- elif match == 'slot_in_description' -%}
      {%- set matched = slot > 0
          and (slot | string) in details | regex_findall('slot\\s*(\\d+)') -%}
    {%- else -%}
      {%- set matched = false -%}
    {%- endif -%}
    {%- set text = match_text | default('', true) | string | lower -%}
    {{ is_state(calendar_entity, 'on') and matched
       and (text == '' or text in title or text in details) }}
  availability: >
    {{ states(calendar_entity) not in ('unknown', 'unavailable') }}

---
blueprint:
  name: "Lock Code Manager: Calendar Condition"
  description: >
    Creates a binary sensor that turns ON when a calendar event is active and
    an optional condition template is truthy. Assign the resulting binary sensor
    as the condition entity for a Lock Code Manager code slot.


    **Available template variables**

    Your condition template can use these variables:

    - `message` — calendar event summary/title

    - `description` — calendar event description

    - `location` — calendar event location

    - `start_time` — event start time

    - `end_time` — event end time

    - `all_day` — whether the event is an all-day event

    - `slot_number` — the resolved slot number

    - `config_entry_title` — the LCM config entry title

    - `name_state` — the current name of the code slot


    **Removed: `lock_entity_ids`**


    This variable no longer exists. It was read off the credential used event
    entity, which used to list the config entry's lock entity IDs as its event
    types and now records one fixed event type instead. Nothing else in Home
    Assistant exposes a config entry's locks to a template, so there is no
    replacement.


    A condition template that still references it fails quietly. Home
    Assistant treats an undefined template variable as empty rather than as
    an error, so the binary sensor stays available, reads `off`, and the PIN
    never activates. The one signal is a line in the Home Assistant log:
    `Template variable warning: 'lock_entity_ids' is undefined when rendering
    ...`. Check the log after upgrading — nothing else will tell you.


    Nothing here can make that louder, and there is nothing worth stubbing
    the variable to: the sensor cannot tell an undefined variable from a
    condition that is honestly false. Nor was the variable worth keeping. The
    list was the same for every slot in the config entry, so
    `{{ 'lock.front_door' in lock_entity_ids }}` could only ever be constantly
    true or constantly false. A Lock Code Manager condition entity gates a
    *user* across every lock in the entry; it cannot gate one lock. Remove the
    reference to fix the sensor.


    **Example condition templates**

    - Allow when event title contains "Guest": `{{ 'Guest' in message }}`

    - Allow when the slot is named for a known guest: `{{ name_state == 'Guest' }}`

    - Match each user against a shared calendar's event:
      `{{ name_state and name_state in message }}`. The `name_state and` matters:
      it is empty when the user's name entity can't be found, and an empty
      string is in every message.


    **When it updates**

    The sensor re-evaluates whenever the calendar's state or current event
    changes, when Home Assistant starts, when template entities reload, and
    once a minute. The minute check catches what the calendar can't signal: a
    user renamed just after their booking starts, or a template that reads the
    time.


    **A condition template that fails to render keeps the sensor where it
    was.** Home Assistant skips the update instead of turning the sensor off,
    so a template that errors once an event ends can leave a PIN active. Give
    filters a default for empty values, e.g. `as_datetime(none)`.


    **Template debugging**

    To test your condition template, go to Developer Tools → Template and paste:

    ```

    {% set message = state_attr('calendar.YOUR_CALENDAR', 'message') | default('', true) %}

    {% set description = state_attr('calendar.YOUR_CALENDAR', 'description') | default('', true) %}

    {% set location = state_attr('calendar.YOUR_CALENDAR', 'location') | default('', true) %}

    {{ YOUR_CONDITION_TEMPLATE_HERE }}

    ```
  domain: template
  # yamllint disable-line rule:line-length
  source_url: https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/blob/main/blueprints/template/lock_code_manager/calendar_condition.yaml
  input:
    config_entry:
      name: Lock Code Manager config entry
      description: The Lock Code Manager config entry that manages your lock(s).
      selector:
        config_entry:
          integration: lock_code_manager
    slot_number:
      name: Slot number
      description: >
        The code slot number. Can be a static number (e.g. `3`) or a Jinja2
        template that resolves to a number using calendar event attributes
        (e.g. `{{ description | regex_findall('slot (\\d+)') | first }}`).
      selector:
        template:
    calendar_entity:
      name: Calendar entity
      description: The calendar entity whose events control this condition.
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: calendar
    condition_template:
      name: Condition template
      description: >
        A Jinja2 template that must evaluate to truthy for the sensor to turn
        ON (in addition to the calendar being active). Leave as `{{ true }}`
        to activate whenever the calendar event is active.
      default: "{{ true }}"
      selector:
        template:

triggers:
  - trigger: state
    entity_id: !input calendar_entity

definition.name: mcp__mcphub-automation__firecrawl-firecrawl_scrape
definition.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content: markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema. Use it when the request identifies a page and needs its content or defined fields: the user gives a URL or names a page or PDF and wants it read or summarized, or wants prices, specs, contact details or a table from it. Use `firecrawl_search` when additional web sources are needed; on an authenticated session, `firecrawl_map` lists a site's URLs and `firecrawl_crawl` collects a set of pages.

Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch or a smaller `maxAge` to bound staleness. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled. Authenticated responses can include a `metadata.scrapeId` for optional scrape feedback.

On an authenticated session, `firecrawl_search` and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching provider returns typed records in one call.

With `alexandria` in place of `url`, the tool runs catalogued provider capabilities instead of fetching a page. Some providers require accepted terms; when a response reports a terms requirement, direct the user to the Firecrawl dashboard URL in that response.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Some providers require accepted terms; when a response reports a terms requirement, direct the user to the Firecrawl dashboard URL in that response.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

definition.name: mcp__mcphub-automation__firecrawl-firecrawl_search
definition.description:
Search web, news, or image sources and return ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Use it for current information, or to list businesses, people, products, jobs or events with websites, prices or contacts. Each web result is a title, URL, and description; use `firecrawl_scrape` on a result URL when the excerpt is not enough.

Authenticated search also returns matching Alexandria data providers in data.tools (companies, people, jobs, finance and filings, public records and government spending, real estate, places and restaurants, retail and prices, package registries and developer data, news, research, and more). Prefer a provider over scraping pages when the task needs the same fields across several entities, exact figures or timestamps, provenance, or many records; use web results when they already answer the question. Authenticated searches always add alexandria to the sources, so sources: ["web"] also returns providers; domainTools: false turns off website-matched tools only.

On an authenticated session, tool matches describe available capabilities; `firecrawl_find_tools` returns their contracts and `firecrawl_scrape` with an `alexandria` body executes a selected capability. Keyless sessions get no Alexandria matches in data.tools.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`; its hits return in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; authenticated sessions also have `firecrawl_gov_search` as the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law. `categories: ["research"]` restricts web results to research-affiliated websites; the `firecrawl_research_*` tools are a separate surface over paper abstracts and full text (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv, arXiv). Returns source-type result groups and usage metadata. Authenticated responses can include an `id` for optional search feedback.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. Authenticated searches always add alexandria to the sources, so sources: ["web"] also returns providers; domainTools: false turns off website-matched tools only. enterprise zdr or anon searches do not add it. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

scrapeOptions.description: Fetches the full page of every web result in the same call, and each fetched result is billed as a scrape. Leave it unset unless the task needs the full text of a few results: highlights usually answer, and firecrawl_scrape can fetch only the URLs you need. These fetches ignore maxAge, so use firecrawl_scrape for a live fetch. scrapeOptions fetches web pages, never Alexandria provider tools.

    hass: HomeAssistant,

    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
    inputs: dict[str, str],
    event: tuple[str, str, str],

    )

async def test_calendar_condition_follows_the_current_event(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    One shared calendar gates each guest by the event that is on now.

    A booking calendar stays ``on`` across back-to-back stays and only its
    event attributes change. When the match was frozen at load, the first
    guest's sensor stayed on through every later booking and the next
    guest's never turned on.
    """
    hass.states.async_set("calendar.bookings", "off", {})
    await _setup_calendar_condition(
        hass,
        lock_code_manager_config_entry,
        "calendar.bookings",
        match="name_in_title",
    )

    assert await _calendar_at(hass, "on", "test1 arriving") == "on"
    assert await _calendar_at(hass, "on", "test2 arriving") == "off"
    assert await _calendar_at(hass, "on", "test1 back again") == "on"
    assert await _calendar_at(hass, "off") == "off"


async def test_calendar_condition_follows_a_rename(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    A user renamed after their booking starts is matched at once.

    Rotating a standing user per booking renames them when the event starts,
    which can land after the calendar change. Nothing about the calendar
    changes again until checkout, so the sensor has to follow the user's name
    entity itself.
    """
    hass.states.async_set("calendar.bookings", "off", {})
    await _setup_calendar_condition(
        hass,
        lock_code_manager_config_entry,
        "calendar.bookings",
        match="name_in_title",
    )
    assert await _calendar_at(hass, "on", "Sarah Chen") == "off"

    await hass.services.async_call(
        TEXT_DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_SET_VALUE,
        service_data={ATTR_VALUE: "Sarah Chen"},
        target={ATTR_ENTITY_ID: SLOT_1_NAME_ENTITY},
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    assert hass.states.get(CALENDAR_CONDITION_ENTITY).state == "on"


async def test_calendar_condition_does_not_match_a_user_it_cannot_find(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    A slot with no name entity matches no event, rather than every event.

    An empty name is in every title, so a name match against a user that
    can't be found (no such slot, or the name entity unavailable and so
    without attributes) would otherwise turn the sensor on for any booking.
    """
    hass.states.async_set("calendar.bookings", "off", {})
    await _setup_calendar_condition(
        hass,
        lock_code_manager_config_entry,
        "calendar.bookings",
        match="name_in_title",
        slot_number=99,
    )

    assert await _calendar_at(hass, "on", "Somebody else") == "off"


async def test_calendar_condition_is_unavailable_with_its_calendar(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """An unavailable calendar makes the sensor unavailable, which LCM treats as inactive."""
    hass.states.async_set("calendar.bookings", "off", {})
    await _setup_calendar_condition(
        hass, lock_code_manager_config_entry, "calendar.bookings", match="any"
    )

    assert await _calendar_at(hass, STATE_UNAVAILABLE) == STATE_UNAVAILABLE


async def test_calendar_condition_from_an_earlier_version_does_not_load(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    caplog,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    A sensor without Match refuses to load instead of guessing one.

    Match has no default on purpose. Defaulting to "any event" would turn a
    sensor that used to filter through its condition template into one that
    is on during every event, so an existing sensor fails closed until its
    owner picks a match: no sensor, so the user's PIN stays inactive.
    """
    hass.states.async_set("calendar.bookings", "on", {"message": "Anything"})
    await _setup_calendar_condition(
        hass,
        lock_code_manager_config_entry,
        "calendar.bookings",
        condition_template="{{ 'Guest' in message }}",
    )

    assert hass.states.get(CALENDAR_CONDITION_ENTITY) is None
    assert "Missing input match" in caplog.text

content.thinking:
I've confirmed MissingInput is a HomeAssistantError rather than a vol.Invalid, and template's loop only catches vol.Invalid — so this error would propagate and break ALL template entities, not just the problematic one. That means a required input without a default could cause anyone re-importing the blueprint without a `match` value to lose every YAML template entity, which is unacceptable.

So "required input fails closed" isn't a safe design — I need `match` to have a default that fails safely per-entity instead. The best approach seems to be making the sensor unavailable when `match` holds an unrecognized value, using an availability template that checks against the known valid options — this fails closed for just that sensor while making the misconfiguration visibly obvious as "unavailable" rather than silently breaking everything.

But I realize this creates a new problem: users who never configured `condition_template` (the common "any event" default case) would now also hit "unavailable" until they pick a match, effectively locking out the majority use case. I think the fix is to keep `condition_template` as a deprecated input with an empty-string default rather than a template default, so I can distinguish users who left it unset from those who explicitly set it — since rendering an unset empty string versus an explicitly-set template produces different output.

So the logic becomes: if match is unset and the legacy template was also never set, behave like before (any event, seamless). If match is unset but the legacy template was explicitly set to something, fail closed to unavailable rather than guessing from a frozen render, since a custom template could render "true" at load time purely by coincidence and falsely appear equivalent to "any." I'm uncertain whether UI-created instances always store input defaults explicitly, which could affect this, but treating any explicitly stored legacy value as grounds for fail-closed seems safest with proper documentation.

I also confirm the catastrophic failure case is real in production code, not just a test artifact — a list with two entries causes the whole thing to fail, which traces back to an actual HA core validation gap that doesn't catch a BlueprintException; I'll just mention this rather than filing it myself.

Now I'm defining the blueprint inputs: a match selector defaulting to an empty string so nothing is preselected in the UI, and a deprecated condition_template input also defaulting to empty, labeled clearly as no longer used with guidance to leave it blank.

I'm working out how to compute an effective match value that falls back to "any" only when both match and the legacy condition are unset, but I realize this needs care since a legacy template could itself render to an empty string, creating an ambiguous edge case where something meant to be set looks unset and silently falls back to "any" when it shouldn't.

I'm settling on using a non-template sentinel string like "unset" as the default for the legacy field, since realistic user templates would almost never render to that exact string, which avoids the ambiguity — though I'll need to relabel the input field so it doesn't look confusing to new users who stumble onto a deprecated option.

I realize "" is genuinely ambiguous since a legitimate template could render to an empty string, which for an access gate could fail open permanently and undermine the whole purpose. That risk, rare as it is, tips me toward using a dedicated sentinel value instead to unambiguously mark "unset."

Now I'm working through the test cases: older configs with a custom legacy condition but no match should leave the sensor unavailable; those with neither should behave like "any"; and when both match and legacy condition exist, match should simply take precedence. I'll update the docs to reflect this and move to implementation.

I've confirmed a real HA limitation: a required `match` input would break every template entity since `MissingInput` isn't caught like `vol.Invalid`. So I'll make `match` default to "not set" instead, keep the legacy `condition_template` input around (defaulted the same way) just to detect old configs, and design the migration so sensors with no condition default to "any event" (unchanged behavior) while sensors with an old custom condition but no match go unavailable rather than silently widening their filter.

### Calendar Condition

Creates a template binary sensor that turns ON when a calendar
event is active and an optional condition template evaluates to
true. Assign the sensor as a user's condition entity to control when
their PIN is active.

- Filter by event title, description, or location using Jinja2 templates
- Supports any HA calendar integration (local, Google, CalDAV, etc.)
- The sensor is unavailable while the calendar entity is `unknown` or
  `unavailable`
- One shared calendar can gate many users: match each user against the
  current event with `{{ name_state and name_state in message }}`. Keep the
  `name_state and`: `name_state` is empty when the user's name entity can't be
  found (for example while all the configuration's locks are unavailable), and
  an empty string is in every message
- The sensor re-evaluates whenever the calendar's state or current event
  changes, when Home Assistant starts, when template entities reload, and once
  a minute. The minute check catches a user renamed just after their booking
  starts, and a template that reads the time
- A condition template that fails to render leaves the sensor where it was:
  Home Assistant skips the update instead of turning it off, so a template
  that errors once an event ends can leave a PIN active. Give filters a
  default for empty values, e.g. `as_datetime(none)`

> **Breaking: `lock_entity_ids` is gone.** It came from the credential used
> event entity, which no longer lists the config entry's locks as its event
> types, and nothing else exposes a config entry's locks to a template.
> **A condition template that still references it fails quietly.** Home
> Assistant treats an undefined template variable as empty rather than as an
> error, so the binary sensor stays available, reads `off`, and the PIN never
> activates. The one signal is a log line — `Template variable warning:
> 'lock_entity_ids' is undefined when rendering ...` — so check the Home
> Assistant log after upgrading. Nothing can make that louder: the sensor
> cannot tell an undefined variable from a condition that is honestly false.
> There is no replacement and nothing worth stubbing it to. The list was
> identical for every slot in the config entry, so
> `{{ 'lock.front_door' in lock_entity_ids }}` could only ever be constantly
> true or constantly false: a condition entity gates a *user* across every
> lock in the entry, and never one lock. Delete the reference to fix the
> sensor.

[![Import Blueprint](https://my.home-assistant.io/badges/blueprint_import.svg)](https://my.home-assistant.io/redirect/blueprint_import/?blueprint_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Framan325%2Flock_code_manager%2Fblob%2Fmain%2Fblueprints%2Ftemplate%2Flock_code_manager%2Fcalendar_condition.yaml)

| Input | Description | Default |
| ----- | ----------- | ------- |
| Lock Code Manager config entry | Config entry holding the user | Required |
| Slot number | The user's slot number (see [Finding a slot number](#finding-a-slot-number)), as a number or a template | Required |
| Calendar entity | Calendar to monitor | Required |
| Condition template | Jinja2 template that must also be true for the sensor to turn on, in addition to the calendar event being active | `{{ true }}` |

**Slot number** can be a static number such as `3`, or a Jinja2 template
that resolves to a number from the calendar event's attributes:

```jinja
{{ description | regex_findall('slot (\\d+)') | first }}
```

The condition template can use these variables:

| Variable | Meaning |
| -------- | ------- |
| `message` | The event's summary (title) |
| `description` | The event's description |
| `location` | The event's location |
| `start_time` | The event's start time |
| `end_time` | The event's end time |
| `all_day` | Whether the event is an all-day event |
| `slot_number` | The resolved slot number |
| `config_entry_title` | The Lock Code Manager config entry's title |

cat > /tmp/pr-cc2.md <<'EOF'
# Breaking change

**The Calendar Condition blueprint no longer takes a free-form condition template.** It has a **Match** choice and an optional **Match text** field instead. After re-importing the blueprint:

- **A sensor that never set a condition template keeps working** as **Any event**, which is what its old default `{{ true }}` meant.
- **A sensor that set its own condition template becomes unavailable**, so its user's PIN stays inactive until you choose a Match. That includes one that spelled out `{{ true }}`: the blueprint can't read the stored template back to tell a default from a real filter.
- **A templated slot number** (for example one read out of the event description) is no longer evaluated per event. Use the **"slot N" in the event description** match with the user's own slot number instead.

**What to do:** re-import the blueprint, then open each Calendar Condition sensor and choose a Match. For a rule the choices don't cover, make your own template binary sensor and use it as the condition entity.

## Proposed change

The Calendar Condition blueprint matched its user against the event that was current when the sensor loaded. A state-based template entity renders its `variables` once at startup (`homeassistant/components/template/template_entity.py:478-481`), and the event attributes, the user's name and the condition result were all variables. On one shared booking calendar, the first guest's sensor stayed on through every later booking, and the next guest's never turned on until template entities were reloaded.

**The fix:** everything that can change now lives in the `state:` template. Home Assistant tracks every entity a state template reads, so the sensor updates as soon as the calendar moves to another event or the user is renamed, with no timer. A render error in `state:` makes the sensor unavailable (`template_entity.py:230-234`), which leaves the PIN inactive.

That rules out a free-form condition template: a blueprint `!input` replaces a whole YAML value (`annotatedyaml/input.py:43-56`), so a user's template can only reach the event through `variables`, which are frozen. The template is replaced by:

| Match | The sensor is on while the current event… |
| --- | --- |
| Any event | is any event |
| User's name in the event title | has the user's name in its title |
| User's name in the event description | has the user's name in its description |
| "slot N" in the event description | says `slot 3`, for the user on slot 3 (`slot 12` doesn't count as `slot 1`) |

**Match text** narrows any of them: the title or description must also contain it. Name and text matching ignore case. A user the sensor can't find (no such slot, or the name entity unavailable and so without attributes) matches no event. An empty name would otherwise be in every title.

**Why Match has a default of "not set" rather than being required:** a blueprint instance missing an input raises `MissingInput`, a `HomeAssistantError` (`blueprint/errors.py:73`). The template integration only skips entries that raise `vol.Invalid` (`template/config.py:444`), so one stale sensor without Match would stop every template entity in the user's configuration from loading. I reproduced this with a second, unrelated template entity. The default instead keeps old sensors that never filtered working, and fails closed only for those that did.

**An earlier version of this PR** made the blueprint trigger-based with a one-minute backstop. Review found it failed open, keeping its last state when a template errored, and it needed the timer. This version needs neither.

**Tests:** `tests/test_blueprint_behavior.py`
- Each Match choice and Match text (14 cases): case-insensitive names, `slot 12` not matching `slot 1`, title versus description, text narrowing a name match.
- Follows a shared calendar from one guest's event to the next and back, with no reload.
- Follows a rename at once.
- A user it can't find matches no event.
- Unavailable with its calendar.
- Upgrade: no condition template → any event; a custom template, or an explicit `{{ true }}` → unavailable; choosing a Match brings a sensor with an old template back.

Mutations checked, each failing at least one test: the empty-name guard, the exact slot match, case-folding, Match text, treating an old template as any event, the availability check on Match, and freezing the event title in `variables` (the original bug).

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [x] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: fixes #
- This PR is related to issue:

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

The reworked blueprint is pushed to #1789 (`b4795d1e`): https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1789. All 65 tests in the blueprint test file pass, along with the websocket tests (207 across both files) and the pre-commit checks. A fresh independent review is running. Don't merge until it reports, since the review of the previous version found two real problems.

**What the blueprint does now:**
- A **Match** dropdown:
  - any event
  - the user's name in the event title
  - the user's name in the event description
  - "slot N" in the event description
- An optional **Match text** field.
- All matching happens in the `state:` template. Home Assistant tracks everything it reads, so the sensor follows the calendar and a rename immediately, with no timer.
- If the template fails to render, the sensor becomes unavailable and the PIN stays inactive.
- Names and text match regardless of case, and "slot 12" doesn't count as "slot 1".

**One change from what we agreed: Match isn't required.** I found that a blueprint instance with a missing input raises an error that the template integration doesn't catch (`template/config.py:444`). One old sensor without Match would stop all of a user's template entities from loading. I reproduced that with a second, unrelated template entity. So Match defaults to "not set" instead:

| Existing sensor | After re-importing |
|---|---|
| Never set a condition template | Keeps working as **Any event**, which is what its old default meant |
| Set its own condition template | Unavailable, so the PIN stays inactive until a Match is chosen |

A sensor that spelled out `{{ true }}` lands in the second row. The blueprint can't read the stored template back to tell a default from a real filter, so it errs toward inactive.

**Decision for you:** this is labeled a breaking change, because sensors with custom templates stop working until they're reconfigured. With your release tagger, that makes the next release 9.0.0. If you'd rather it go out as a minor release with an upgrade note, tell me and I'll take the Breaking change section out.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The safer-sounding plan of a required input would have been the most damaging, because of a gap in Home Assistant. Running the failure with a second, unrelated entity showed it wouldn't fail on its own: it would have taken every template entity down with it.
- The mutations checked each guard: the empty-name check, the exact slot match, case-folding, Match text, the upgrade logic, and freezing the title in variables, which was the original bug. Each one broke at least one test, so none of those guards is decorative.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

There's also a Home Assistant core bug here: the template integration should skip an instance with a missing blueprint input the same way it skips other invalid entries. That one's yours to report, if you want to.
